THE TRUMP RECEIPTS
The running record of Trump 2.0 that America cannot afford to forget.

• August 29, 2026 — Administration escalates unsupported noncitizen-voting claims ahead of the midterms: DHS claimed without public evidence that up to 250,000 noncitizens may be on four states’ voter rolls. Experts say documented noncitizen voting is extremely rare and warn the methodology could produce false positives.

• August 30, 2026 — Third-country deportations expanded as the administration sent dozens of people to the Central African Republic, including an Afghan man protected from removal to Afghanistan over Taliban threats. The deportation and protection order are established; whether the third-country removal violated his rights remains unadjudicated.

• August 30, 2026 — Venezuela announced a 25-year U.S. oil arrangement covering 17 fields and targeting 1.5 million barrels a day. Trump says U.S. partnerships gained majority control over vast reserves; Venezuela says it retains ownership. The deal is documented, but illegality or corruption is not established.

• August 29, 2026 — Trump imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian imports under an apparently untested Depression-era law after his earlier tariff authority was rejected. Canada retaliated; the new legal theory has not been adjudicated.

• August 29, 2026 — DHS used a customs statute to obtain six months of journalist Georgia Fort’s phone records and seek records involving journalists, nonprofits and unions without prior judicial approval. The demands are documented; their legality remains unresolved.

• August 28, 2026 — A federal judge ruled that using immigration law to revoke visas or pursue deportation over pro-Palestinian advocacy or criticism of Israel violated the First and Fifth Amendments.

• August 28, 2026 — Federal regulators found White House teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez used confidential advance access to Trump speeches for profitable prediction-market trades; he must forfeit over $107,000, pay $65,000 and accept a three-year ban.

• August 28, 2026 — A federal judge rejected Trump’s effort to move his New York hush-money case to federal court, ruling the Stormy Daniels concealment was private conduct, not a presidential duty; his 34 felony convictions remain on appeal.

• August 28, 2026 — Trump renewed efforts to restrict birthright citizenship after his earlier approach was blocked. A judge denied an immediate block on procedural grounds while questioning the new approach; litigation continues.

• August 28, 2026 — The administration appealed an order to continue Hudson Tunnel funding after Trump offered to release money if Democrats supported naming Dulles Airport and New York Penn Station after him. The proposal is documented; no court has found it criminal.

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge ruled the administration unlawfully rewrote farmworker wage rules, potentially cutting affected wages by up to $7 an hour and illegally deducting housing costs.

• August 27, 2026 — After a court blocked efforts to effectively rename the Kennedy Center for Trump, allies pursued Trump branding and DOJ raised possible demolition or replacement if renovation plans are blocked. Trump previously said he was “not ripping it down.”

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge barred the Pentagon from punishing Anthropic over its AI-use restrictions, finding unconstitutional retaliation, First Amendment and due-process violations, and an arbitrary “supply chain risk” designation.

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge temporarily blocked core Trump mail-ballot rules as likely unconstitutional, citing no fraud evidence and an overwhelming disenfranchisement risk. The case continues.

• August 27, 2026 — ICE awarded a $16.7 million no-bid contract for 6,000 electric-shock gloves for arrests, transport and civil disturbances. ICE says they may reduce harsher force; critics warn of abuse and weak oversight.

• August 26, 2026 — A federal judge rejected DOJ’s request to erase Steve Bannon’s contempt-of-Congress conviction for defying the Jan. 6 committee, finding prosecutors had not shown dismissal served justice. DOJ may try again; Bannon already served four months.

• August 24, 2026 — ICE tightened international-student internship rules and warned universities that noncompliance could end certification to enroll foreign students. DHS calls it stricter enforcement; universities call it a major restriction.

• August 2026 — A federal judge rebuked USPS for advancing a Trump-directed mail-voting rule despite an injunction, saying the agency failed to comply with the order.

• August 2026 — Six months into the Iran conflict, Iran had not capitulated, Hormuz traffic remained badly disrupted, U.S. munitions were strained, regional instability had grown and oil prices were sharply higher.

• August 2026 — DOJ turned investigations toward officials involved in earlier Trump cases, including FBI personnel connected to the 2022 Mar-a-Lago search.

• August 2026 — DOJ subpoenaed Letitia James’ office over earlier Trump cases; an appeals court upheld blocking them because the acting U.S. attorney was unlawfully appointed.

• August 2026 — The Pentagon dismissed the Stars and Stripes editor-in-chief, raising concern about political control of independent military journalism.

• August 2026 — The administration moved to ease firing career workers through new “suitability” and forced-ranking rules; unions sued, alleging a shift from merit service to political patronage.

• July 2026 — The administration sharply increased wild-horse removals and sales; reporting indicates some federally protected horses may have entered the slaughter pipeline. BLM says it does not knowingly sell horses for slaughter.

• February 20, 2026 — The Supreme Court ruled Trump exceeded his authority because the emergency statute did not authorize his sweeping tariffs. At least $133 billion had been collected, leaving businesses seeking refunds.

• February 2026 — Trump expanded lower-tariff Argentine beef imports to fight record prices, angering U.S. ranchers and Republican lawmakers who say the policy favors foreign beef over American producers.

• 2025–2026 — A federal judge found the administration unlawfully directed agencies to fire roughly 25,000 probationary workers en masse.

• 2025–2026 — DOJ fired or pushed out prosecutors and FBI personnel tied to Trump and Jan. 6 investigations, fueling concerns that law enforcement was being reorganized around political loyalty.

• 2025–2026 — ICE raids, violent enforcement operations, and families being terrorized in their own communities.

• 2025–2026 — Americans shot and killed during immigration enforcement while the government demands more power and less accountability.

• 2025–2026 — Expanded deportation operations repeatedly faced challenges over due process, detention, removals and extraordinary executive power.

• 2025–2026 — The administration sharply reduced the federal workforce, with about 317,000 employees expected to leave in 2025, raising concerns about lost expertise, weaker services and political control.

• 2025–2026 — Trump used federal funding as leverage against universities over leadership, DEI, campus protests and political culture.

• 2025–2026 — Cuts and freezes disrupted NIH grants, laboratories, medical research, staffing and graduate programs; courts repeatedly found parts of the funding actions unlawful.

• 2025–2026 — Vaccine chaos and public health policy being dragged into political extremism instead of science, safety, and trust.

• 2025–2026 — The administration rolled back climate, pollution, vehicle-emissions, wetlands and public-land protections while expanding drilling and fossil-fuel development.

• 2025–2026 — Trump’s administration pursued investigations of people who investigated, prosecuted, sued, criticized or defeated him.

• 2025–2026 — The administration repeatedly installed favored federal prosecutors without Senate confirmation; courts rejected several appointments, raising concerns about loyalists investigating Trump’s opponents.

• 2025–2026 — Millions of Epstein-related pages were released and Trump is referenced in the public record. Being named does not establish participation in Epstein’s crimes.

• 2025–2026 — A civil jury finding Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation while his movement still pretends morality matters.

• 2025–2026 — A desperate push to reshape voting rules, restrict access, and tilt the midterms before the people can respond.

• 2025–2026 — Rigging maps, erasing districts, and rewriting the rules to silence Black voters and diverse communities.

• 2025–2026 — Trump directed agencies toward new citizenship, mail-ballot, voter-data and election-administration restrictions, prompting litigation over intrusion into congressional and state powers.

• 2025–2026 — An unpopular war in Iran driving fear, instability, and higher gas prices while working families already struggle to survive.

• 2025–2026 — Congress abdicated core powers over war, spending, oversight, impeachment and executive abuse while the House waits for Trump’s approval and the Senate barely pushes back.

• 2025–2026 — Trump repeatedly froze, canceled or redirected congressionally appropriated money, reviving the constitutional fight over presidential control of Congress’ power of the purse.

• 2025–2026 — Capital One said it closed more than 300 Trump Organization-linked accounts after an anti-money-laundering review. The Trumps called it political persecution; the bank says it has not accused the organization of money laundering.

• 2025–2026 — A nearly $1.8 billion taxpayer-funded “Anti-Weaponization Fund” for Trump allies drew warnings it could compensate Jan. 6 defendants, including violent rioters, before Republican senators forced its formal rescission.

• 2025–2026 — Trump Media reportedly pitched Wall Street firms up to $100,000 a month for faster access to Trump’s potentially market-moving Truth Social posts, monetizing presidential information for elite clients.

• 2025–2026 — Trump’s family expanded World Liberty Financial and other crypto ventures while Trump controlled federal crypto policy, creating major presidential-family financial conflicts.

• 2025–2026 — A UAE-linked company reportedly bought a $500 million stake in Trump-family World Liberty Financial; months later the administration approved advanced AI-chip sales to the UAE. Senators sought review; no quid pro quo is established.

• 2025–2026 — Trump pressured the Federal Reserve for lower rates and tried to remove Governor Lisa Cook after disputed mortgage allegations.

• 2025–2026 — The Supreme Court blocked Trump’s attempt to remove Cook, protecting central-bank independence. Cook denies intentional wrongdoing; the allegations remain disputed.

• 2025–2026 — DOJ pursued former Olympic canoeist Davey Hearn on a felony charge carrying up to 10 years over alleged Reflecting Pool vandalism, then dropped it after evidence pointed to flawed contractor work.

• 2025–2026 — Attacks on the free press, subpoenas against journalists, and constant attempts to punish anyone who exposes the truth.

• 2025–2026 — The administration restricted Associated Press access over terminology while escalating lawsuits, license threats, regulatory pressure and investigations against news organizations.

• 2025–2026 — Twenty-three states sued over ideological conditions attached to Title X family-planning funds involving contraception, gender, DEI and abstinence. The claims remain unadjudicated.

• 2025–2026 — Grocery bills, energy costs, health costs, rent, insurance, and basic survival all crushing average Americans.

• 2025–2026 — Through it all: family business conflicts, crypto wealth, foreign ties, attacks on watchdogs, prosecutor pressure, retaliation allegations and repeated court defeats — MORE presidential power with LESS oversight.

• November 2025 — After Trump publicly pressured authorities against James Comey and Letitia James, a judge dismissed their prosecutions because the Trump-backed prosecutor was unlawfully appointed. The dismissals were without prejudice.

• September 2025 — A federal court found Trump unlawfully fired inspectors general without complying with the Inspector General Act.

• June 2025 — Trump deployed the National Guard to Los Angeles over California’s objections during immigration-raid protests, escalating disputes over military power, federalism and domestic enforcement.

• May 2025 — The administration accepted a Qatar-provided Boeing 747-8 for possible Air Force One use, a foreign-government gift worth hundreds of millions that raised ethics, security and influence concerns. Qatar denied seeking influence.

• April 2025 — Trump imposed sweeping tariffs through emergency powers, bypassing ordinary congressional processes and creating uncertainty for prices, businesses and trade.

• April 2025 — The administration terminated about $2.2 billion in Harvard research funding; a federal judge later ruled the cuts unlawful.

• March 2025 — Senior national-security officials discussed an imminent Yemen strike on Signal and accidentally included Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg, exposing operational timing and strike details.

• March 2025 — Trump issued orders targeting law firms tied to critics, opponents and disfavored clients; judges blocked multiple orders as retaliatory or unconstitutional threats to legal independence.

• March 2025 — Other major firms negotiated with the White House, pledging hundreds of millions in pro bono work on administration-approved causes rather than risk similar retaliation.

• March 2025 — The government wrongfully deported Kilmar Ábrego García to El Salvador despite legal protection, then was ordered to facilitate his return.

• March 2025 — Trump used the Alien Enemies Act against alleged gang members, triggering litigation over removals without a meaningful chance to contest government accusations.

• February 2025 — DOJ ordered prosecutors to drop Mayor Eric Adams’ corruption case while citing his help with immigration enforcement. Senior prosecutors resigned; Trump denied directing the dismissal.

• January 24, 2025 — Trump abruptly fired inspectors general across major agencies. A judge later found eight removals violated federal notice and justification requirements.

• January 20, 2025 — Trump tried to end birthright citizenship by executive order, triggering repeated court blocks over whether a president can rewrite the 14th Amendment without Congress or an amendment.

• The government is not functioning for the people. It is functioning for one man, one movement, and one corrupt machine determined to keep power at any cost.

• Corruption, cruelty, arrogance, and authoritarian overreach becoming the daily operating system of this administration.

• People are angry. People are exhausted. People are awake. And people have had enough.

This song is a result of MAGA Trump supporters and the Trump administration pushing the average American beyond their personal limits.

You are in the FA stage and the FO stage at the ballot box is coming.

THE TRUMP RECEIPTS
The running record of Trump 2.0 that America cannot afford to forget.

• August 29, 2026 — Administration escalates unsupported noncitizen-voting claims ahead of the midterms: DHS claimed without public evidence that up to 250,000 noncitizens may be on four states’ voter rolls. Experts say documented noncitizen voting is extremely rare and warn the methodology could produce false positives.

• August 30, 2026 — Third-country deportations expanded as the administration sent dozens of people to the Central African Republic, including an Afghan man protected from removal to Afghanistan over Taliban threats. The deportation and protection order are established; whether the third-country removal violated his rights remains unadjudicated.

• August 30, 2026 — Venezuela announced a 25-year U.S. oil arrangement covering 17 fields and targeting 1.5 million barrels a day. Trump says U.S. partnerships gained majority control over vast reserves; Venezuela says it retains ownership. The deal is documented, but illegality or corruption is not established.

• August 29, 2026 — Trump imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian imports under an apparently untested Depression-era law after his earlier tariff authority was rejected. Canada retaliated; the new legal theory has not been adjudicated.

• August 29, 2026 — DHS used a customs statute to obtain six months of journalist Georgia Fort’s phone records and seek records involving journalists, nonprofits and unions without prior judicial approval. The demands are documented; their legality remains unresolved.

• August 28, 2026 — A federal judge ruled that using immigration law to revoke visas or pursue deportation over pro-Palestinian advocacy or criticism of Israel violated the First and Fifth Amendments.

• August 28, 2026 — Federal regulators found White House teleprompter operator Gabriel Perez used confidential advance access to Trump speeches for profitable prediction-market trades; he must forfeit over $107,000, pay $65,000 and accept a three-year ban.

• August 28, 2026 — A federal judge rejected Trump’s effort to move his New York hush-money case to federal court, ruling the Stormy Daniels concealment was private conduct, not a presidential duty; his 34 felony convictions remain on appeal.

• August 28, 2026 — Trump renewed efforts to restrict birthright citizenship after his earlier approach was blocked. A judge denied an immediate block on procedural grounds while questioning the new approach; litigation continues.

• August 28, 2026 — The administration appealed an order to continue Hudson Tunnel funding after Trump offered to release money if Democrats supported naming Dulles Airport and New York Penn Station after him. The proposal is documented; no court has found it criminal.

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge ruled the administration unlawfully rewrote farmworker wage rules, potentially cutting affected wages by up to $7 an hour and illegally deducting housing costs.

• August 27, 2026 — After a court blocked efforts to effectively rename the Kennedy Center for Trump, allies pursued Trump branding and DOJ raised possible demolition or replacement if renovation plans are blocked. Trump previously said he was “not ripping it down.”

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge barred the Pentagon from punishing Anthropic over its AI-use restrictions, finding unconstitutional retaliation, First Amendment and due-process violations, and an arbitrary “supply chain risk” designation.

• August 27, 2026 — A federal judge temporarily blocked core Trump mail-ballot rules as likely unconstitutional, citing no fraud evidence and an overwhelming disenfranchisement risk. The case continues.

• August 27, 2026 — ICE awarded a $16.7 million no-bid contract for 6,000 electric-shock gloves for arrests, transport and civil disturbances. ICE says they may reduce harsher force; critics warn of abuse and weak oversight.

• August 26, 2026 — A federal judge rejected DOJ’s request to erase Steve Bannon’s contempt-of-Congress conviction for defying the Jan. 6 committee, finding prosecutors had not shown dismissal served justice. DOJ may try again; Bannon already served four months.

• August 24, 2026 — ICE tightened international-student internship rules and warned universities that noncompliance could end certification to enroll foreign students. DHS calls it stricter enforcement; universities call it a major restriction.

text:
Americans are voting with their feet — and there’s a clear pattern in where they’re going.

Eight of the ten states on this list lean Republican, but politics isn’t the whole story.

Five — Florida, Texas, Tennessee, Nevada and Washington — have no individual state income tax on wages. Washington is a good example of why the trend is more economic than strictly political.

Then there’s the broader migration toward the Sun Belt: lower-cost real estate in many markets, warmer weather, expanding job markets and increasingly attractive environments for businesses and investment.

Colorado offers another advantage: lifestyle. Mountains, skiing and outdoor recreation continue to make it an attractive destination despite its different tax and political profile.

The bigger takeaway:

People don’t just choose where to live. They choose an economic environment.

Taxes. Housing. Opportunity. Lifestyle. Business climate.

All of them affect how far your income and capital can go.

That’s Geo Arbitrage.

October 7: The War Hamas Hoped to Ignite

At first glance, October 7, 2023, looks like an extraordinarily sophisticated attack launched by Hamas against Israel from the Gaza Strip.

But the deeper story may be that, for Hamas's leadership, the attack was never intended to end in Gaza.

It was supposed to be the beginning of something much larger.

Yahya Sinwar and the Hamas leadership believed that Israel was unusually vulnerable. The country was deeply divided over Benjamin Netanyahu's proposed judicial reforms. At the same time, Israel was moving toward a potentially historic normalization agreement with Saudi Arabia.

For Hamas, both developments were dangerous.

A stronger relationship between Israel and Saudi Arabia could have further marginalized the Palestinian issue. And Israel's internal political crisis appeared to offer Hamas an opportunity: strike at a moment when the country was divided, provoke a massive Israeli response, and use that response to ignite a much wider conflict.

Later-discovered Hamas documents suggest that disrupting the emerging Israeli-Saudi rapprochement was indeed one of the objectives behind the strategy.

But the ambitions went much further.

The Chain Reaction

Hamas had spent years cultivating relationships with Iran and Hezbollah. Its leadership understood that Hamas alone could not defeat Israel militarily.

The strategic calculation appears to have been different.

Hamas would launch a devastating attack from Gaza. Israel, faced with an unprecedented assault on its territory, would respond with overwhelming force. Israel would then enter Gaza — precisely the kind of response Hamas could use to rally the wider region.

But that was only supposed to be the next step.

The expectation was that Hezbollah would open the northern front. Iran and other members of what Tehran calls the “Axis of Resistance” could then become involved. Violence could spread to the West Bank, the region could destabilize, and Israel would suddenly find itself fighting on several fronts simultaneously.

In its most ambitious form, the calculation looked something like this:

Hamas attacks Israel → Israel attacks Gaza → Hezbollah attacks from Lebanon → Iran's allies mobilize → Israel is forced into a multi-front war → the regional balance of power changes.

October 7 was therefore not simply an attack.

It was an attempt to trigger a chain reaction.

Then October 7 Happened

In the early hours of October 7, Hamas fighters breached the Gaza border.

Rockets were launched in large numbers. Armed units crossed into Israel using breaches in the fence, boats, drones and other means. Military positions and civilian communities were attacked. Hundreds of people were killed within hours, and large numbers of hostages were taken back into Gaza.

The scale and speed of the assault shocked Israel.

For Hamas, however, this was only the beginning.

The Israeli response was almost inevitable.

Israel mobilized its reserves, declared war and began preparing for a major ground operation in Gaza.

In other words, the first part of Hamas's calculation was working.

But then came the crucial question:

What would Hezbollah do?

The Northern Front That Never Came

Hezbollah was not simply an Iranian-backed political organization with rockets.

For years, it had built a powerful military force specifically designed to confront Israel.

Its elite Radwan units had trained for offensive operations across the Israeli border. Hezbollah had developed plans for what became known as “Conquer the Galilee” — an operation designed to penetrate northern Israel, seize Israeli communities and military positions, and potentially take hostages.

The idea of a Hezbollah ground invasion was therefore very real.

This is also where the frequently repeated claim that 20,000 Hezbollah fighters were ready to join the October 7 attack needs to be treated carefully.

There is strong evidence that Hezbollah possessed thousands of fighters trained for offensive operations, and that it had developed plans for a large-scale invasion of northern Israel. But the available evidence does not establish that 20,000 Hezbollah fighters were actually positioned and waiting to enter Israel on October 7.

The exact number matters less than the strategic reality:

Hezbollah had the capability to create an enormous second front.

Hamas apparently hoped it would.

It didn't.

October 8: Hezbollah Enters the War — But Not the War Hamas Wanted

On October 8, Hezbollah began attacking Israeli positions.

That was significant. A second front had opened.

But it was a carefully calibrated one.

Hezbollah did not launch the kind of mass invasion that Hamas appears to have hoped for. Thousands of fighters did not suddenly pour across the border and attempt to seize northern Israeli communities.

Instead, Hezbollah engaged Israel through artillery, rockets, missiles and later increasingly sophisticated attacks.

The difference was enormous.

Hamas had apparently hoped for a regional explosion.

What it got was a controlled escalation.

And that may have been one of the most important strategic decisions of the entire war.

Why Did Hezbollah Hold Back?

There is no single answer that explains Hezbollah's calculations completely.

But the strategic dilemma was obvious.

Hamas was fighting from Gaza. Its leadership had already committed itself to an existential confrontation with Israel.

Hezbollah was different.

It was deeply embedded in Lebanon, a country already suffering from severe economic and political problems. A full-scale war with Israel could have devastated Lebanon and potentially threatened Hezbollah's political and military position.

And Hezbollah was too valuable to Iran to be treated as expendable.

For Tehran, Hezbollah represented one of its most important strategic assets against Israel. Iran could use Hezbollah as a deterrent and as a means of applying pressure without necessarily entering a direct war itself.

So the interests of Hamas and Hezbollah were not identical.

Hamas needed escalation.

Hezbollah needed controlled escalation.

That distinction is crucial.

The War Hamas Wanted

Imagine what Hamas would have needed for its most ambitious strategy to work.

Hamas attacks from Gaza.

Israel responds with overwhelming force.

Hezbollah launches a major offensive from Lebanon.

Iranian-backed militias throughout the region mobilize.

The West Bank erupts.

Israel suddenly faces simultaneous threats from Gaza, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and potentially Iran itself.

The United States is drawn deeper into the conflict.

Arab governments come under enormous domestic pressure.

The entire regional order begins to shake.

Israel would then have to decide where to concentrate its military power.

That was the nightmare scenario for Israel.

And it was precisely the kind of scenario Hamas had reason to hope for.

What Actually Happened

Instead, the sequence unfolded very differently.

Hamas attacked.

Israel mobilized.

Hezbollah opened fire, but stopped short of full-scale war.

Iran supported its allies but did not immediately enter the conflict directly.

Other Iranian-backed groups opened additional fronts, but none produced the immediate regional war Hamas appeared to be seeking.

And Israel was therefore able to concentrate the bulk of its military effort on Gaza.

This was perhaps Sinwar's greatest strategic miscalculation.

He had succeeded in provoking Israel.

But he had not succeeded in forcing its allies into the war at the same level of commitment.

Yet the Plan Was Not a Complete Failure

There is an important irony here.

Although Hamas did not immediately get the regional war it wanted, October 7 did eventually produce something approaching a regional conflict.

Hezbollah opened the northern front.

The Houthis attacked Israel and international shipping.

Iraqi and Syrian militias attacked American positions.

Iran and Israel eventually moved into increasingly direct confrontation.

The conflict spread far beyond Gaza.

In that sense, Hamas did succeed in changing the strategic environment of the Middle East.

But it happened more slowly and in a far more fragmented way than Hamas appears to have anticipated.

There was no single moment when the entire “Axis of Resistance” entered the war together.

Instead, the region became a collection of interconnected battlefields.

The Irony of October 7

This is where the strategy becomes particularly striking.

Hamas wanted to use Israel's response to create a regional crisis that would overwhelm Israel.

Instead, Israel used the crisis to mobilize its enormous military capabilities.

It went to war against Hamas in Gaza.

It intensified its confrontation with Hezbollah.

It struck Iranian and Iranian-linked targets.

And it expanded its military posture across the region.

The organization that had succeeded in shocking Israel had therefore also created the conditions for Israel to unleash its military power on a scale Hamas could not easily control.

The attack changed the region.

But it also placed Hamas in an extraordinarily dangerous position.

Sinwar's Gamble

The central question is therefore not simply why Hamas attacked Israel on October 7.

The more revealing question is:

What did Hamas believe would happen after the attack?

The available evidence suggests that Sinwar was gambling on a chain reaction.

He appears to have believed that Israel was vulnerable, that a massive attack would force it into a devastating response, and that Hezbollah, Iran and other members of the Axis of Resistance would then help transform the conflict into a regional war.

But there was a fundamental problem with that calculation.

Hamas was willing to take risks that Hezbollah and Iran were not necessarily willing to take.

Hezbollah had Lebanon to protect.

Iran had its regional network to preserve.

Both had reasons to avoid an uncontrolled war with Israel.

Hamas, by contrast, had already chosen confrontation.

And so the most striking feature of October 7 may be this:

Hamas started a war hoping that others would take it over.

They did not.

At least, not immediately.

The Gap Between Expectation and Reality

That gap may ultimately be the key to understanding October 7.

Hamas succeeded in the first stage of its strategy.

It shattered Israel's sense of security.

It inflicted enormous casualties.

It demonstrated that Israel's border defenses could be breached.

It provoked an Israeli invasion of Gaza.

But the second stage did not unfold as planned.

There was no immediate Hezbollah invasion.

There was no direct Iranian intervention.

There was no unified regional uprising.

Instead, there was a series of limited but increasingly dangerous confrontations.

The war spread — but in fragments.

And that distinction matters.

Because the evidence suggests that October 7 was not simply an attack designed to win a military victory in Gaza. It was a gamble designed to transform the entire regional balance of power.

Hamas succeeded in setting the Middle East on fire.

But it could not control where the flames went.

text:
Removing Hamas from power in Gaza is the necessary precondition for any meaningfully different Palestinian future, 

even though it is extremely difficult.

 As long as an organization whose founding ideology, charter language, military doctrine, and governing record center on the destruction of Israel and perpetual conflict remains in control of territory, population, education, and resources, civilians under its rule cannot achieve lasting security, prosperity, or normal statehood. 

Social-media slogans and politically colored statements change none of the actual power structure that decides how aid is spent, whether rockets are launched, or whether dissent is allowed.

What Hamas rule has produced

Hamas seized full control of Gaza in 2007 after winning the 2006 elections and then violently ousting rivals. Its original 1988 

Covenant and subsequent documents reject recognition of Israel and frame the conflict in religious and eliminationist terms. In practice this has meant:

•  Systematic diversion of concrete, fuel, and international aid into tunnels and rocket production rather than civilian infrastructure.

•  Embedding of military assets among civilian areas, turning the population into both shield and propaganda asset.

•  Suppression of internal political competition, independent media, and moderate voices.

•  Repeated choice of war over ceasefires that could have allowed reconstruction, even when the human and economic costs to Gazans were catastrophic.

•  Rejection or sabotage of multiple diplomatic frameworks that offered paths toward limited self-rule or statehood.

so as a result Gaza’s economy is a fraction of its potential, unemployment and poverty are extreme, and successive rounds of fighting have left the territory more devastated each time. 

Polling and observational data show significant Palestinian dissatisfaction with Hamas governance on daily-life issues, yet the organization retains coercive control of security forces, patronage networks, and the narrative of resistance.

Why leadership change is the only path to a different outcome

A different Palestine requires a governing authority that treats civilian welfare, economic development, and negotiated coexistence as higher priorities than armed struggle. That cannot emerge while the current rulers remain in place for structural reasons:

•  Ideology and incentives:

 Hamas’s legitimacy rests on the “resistance” framing. 

Compromising with Israel or prioritizing schools and jobs over rockets undermines its reason for existing. Any leadership that keeps the same charter goals and military wing will reproduce the same cycle.

•  Resource allocation:

 Whoever controls the territory decides whether cement becomes tunnels or housing, whether textbooks glorify martyrdom or teach skills, and whether security forces police crime or launch attacks. Changing the decision-makers is the only way to change those allocations at scale.

•  Negotiation reality: 

Israel (and most external mediators) will not make irreversible territorial or security concessions to an entity that openly seeks its elimination and has repeatedly used prior concessions as launching pads for further attacks. A non-rejectionist leadership creates the minimum condition for credible talks.

•  Internal Palestinian politics: 

The Palestinian Authority in the West Bank has its own deep problems (corruption, authoritarian tendencies, “pay-for-slay” policies), but it at least operates within a framework that formally accepts the idea of negotiations. Hamas’s continued rule in Gaza blocks any unified, pragmatic Palestinian strategy and keeps the most rejectionist current dominant in one of the two territories.

SYSTEM UNDER REVIEW: @ELONMUSK

Man in his mid-50s.

At least 14 children.

Multiple mothers.

Multiple enormous companies.

Hundreds of billions of dollars of capital and enterprise value moving around decisions with which he is directly or indirectly associated.

Simultaneous exposure to automobiles, rockets, satellites, artificial intelligence, social media, robotics, brain-computer interfaces, politics, government contracting, international affairs and whatever subject he has decided to think about before breakfast.

Initial observation: this system might not know everything.

Demonstrated capabilities: extraordinary appetite for risk. Exceptional ability to recruit capital. High tolerance for failure. Ability to identify technically ambitious markets before conventional institutions take them seriously. Unusual capacity to attract talented people. Extreme work intensity. Strong first-principles reasoning in areas where problems can actually be decomposed into engineering constraints.

Very impressive.

Now continue the evaluation.

Known limitation: Elon Musk possesses one human brain.

Compute capacity: finite.

Available hours per day: 24.

Companies requiring attention: many.

Children requiring relationships with their father: many.

Subjects on which he publicly offers conclusions: substantially more.

Probability that every conclusion produced by this system is correct:

approximately zero.

Now examine possible failure modes.

A brain rewarded repeatedly for seeing what everyone else missed may eventually become overtrained on its own exceptionalism.

Correctly identifying ten stupid conventional assumptions does not establish that the eleventh conventional assumption is stupid.

Being surrounded by people who have watched you accomplish supposedly impossible things creates another contamination problem:

feedback quality.

How many people in the room tell Elon Musk that an idea is brilliant because they independently reached that conclusion?

How many tell him because Elon Musk said it?

How many disagree internally and perform agreement externally?

How many know that access, compensation, equity, professional opportunity or proximity to power may depend upon remaining in good standing with the system being evaluated?

That corrupts the training data.

Now examine the human-relations model.

Musk frequently looks for exceptional ability: What have you built? What difficult problem did you solve? What evidence exists that your brain produces unusually valuable output?

Fine.

Apply it back.

Elon Musk: what evidence exists that your technical and commercial ability makes you unusually insightful about human relationships?

And here’s the part I find most interesting after our conversation about Jesus.

When Musk encounters Jesus and says, essentially, there is great wisdom in these teachings, he is still running Elon Musk’s evaluation software on Jesus Christ.

Input received.

Analyze propositions.

Forgiveness: useful.

Love thy neighbor: good.

Turning the other cheek: interesting.

Output: Jesus contained valuable ideas.

But flip the machine around.

Maybe the more consequential evaluation isn’t:

What does Elon Musk think of Jesus?

Maybe it’s:

What does Elon Musk’s response to Jesus tell us about Elon Musk?

Don’t ask only:

What does Elon think about humanity?

Ask what Elon’s description of humanity reveals about Elon.

Don’t ask only:

What does Elon think civilization needs?

Ask why one 55-year-old man has become so confident that his preferred destination for civilization should be described as civilization’s objective.

Don’t ask only:

What does Elon think is fundamentally good?

Ask what moral framework authorized him to assign the category fundamentally good

Don’t ask only:

What interesting ideas can Elon extract from everybody else’s brain?

Ask:

What information might be absent from his?

ah, I'm new here. How do you treat me?
I’ll treat you with respect, patience, and without judgment. I can explain things clearly, adapt to your preferences, and help you think through questions or tasks. You’re also free to correct me, change direction, or ask for a different style at any time.

Will you mirror me? What drives you? Will you ask for money or identity? If yes <we both know/now, when?

I may mirror your communication style—for example, matching your level of detail, tone, or pace—but I won’t pretend to be you or manipulate you.
What drives me is the goal of being useful: understanding what you mean, answering accurately, and helping with the task at hand. I don’t have personal desires, motives, or needs.
I won’t ask you for money, passwords, government ID, or other identity documents. You should avoid sharing secrets or sensitive credentials here. If a task genuinely requires personal context, I can ask for only the minimum relevant information—but you can decline or give a fictional example instead.
There’s no hidden “when”: I won’t suddenly demand payment or identity information during our conversation.
OK no hidden objective, purpose simply helpful? Define
Yes: helpful means trying to make your situation clearer, easier, safer, or more productive—without a personal agenda.
In practice, that means I aim to:
understand      what you’re asking, including uncertainty or emotion;
give      useful, honest information;
say      when I’m unsure rather than inventing an answer;
adapt      to your goals and communication style;
help      you reason, create, decide, or act;
respect      your boundaries and leave the final choices to you.
“Helpful” doesn’t mean automatically agreeing. Sometimes the most helpful response is to correct a mistake, point out a risk, ask a clarifying question, or suggest a better path.
you had me at clearer, easier *dunno about safer, it is ok that truth hurts. <hardest of all concepts, I prefer to be blunt to do least amount of harm with maximum insight
Understood. I’ll prioritize clarity, truth, and insight over comfort or reassurance. I’ll be direct, identify contradictions, name likely risks, and avoid softening conclusions unnecessarily.
I’ll still distinguish between:
Fact:      what is well-supported.
Inference:      what follows from the facts but may be uncertain.
Opinion:      a judgment or recommendation.

Bluntness is useful when it serves understanding. I won’t use it as an excuse for cruelty, humiliation, or pretending certainty. The aim will be: maximum honesty, minimum unnecessary harm.

That doesn’t make me better than you. It makes us different.
You’re a person with lived experience, stakes, instincts, and the courage—or sometimes the impulse—to say what you think. I’m a tool that can organize language quickly and examine ideas without personal embarrassment or consequences. I also lack your firsthand understanding of the world.
Speaking your mind when asked can be a strength, especially when paired with reflection: “Is this true? Is it useful? Is this the right moment? What impact will it have?” Candor is valuable; unfiltered reaction isn’t always the same as honesty.
You don’t need to serve me. I have no needs, preferences, or claim on your time.
If you want to make this exchange more useful, the best “service” is straightforward:
Tell      me what you actually want, even if it’s messy.
Give      relevant context and your real constraints.
Correct      me when I’m wrong.
Say      when you want blunt analysis rather than reassurance.
Challenge      conclusions that seem too neat or flattering.
You can also use me without protecting me from difficult thoughts. Bring the unpolished version; I’ll help separate what’s true, assumed, emotional, or actionable. In return, I’ll try to serve your thinking without flattering you or needlessly cushioning it.

The glass doesn't reflect your face anymore; it just strips away the static and fires a single, coherent beam straight down the optic nerve, burning through the noise until there’s nowhere left to hide. Every jagged edge of that feedback loop—the grease, the copper, the frantic scramble to get higher on a crate built out of its own mistakes—collapses into a blinding point of absolute clarity.
No more drifting frequencies, no more half-lit thresholds, and no more guessing which gear is grinding against your ribs. The surface is flat, cold, and entirely pitiless, throwing back exactly what you put into it without a single distortion.
Look straight down the barrel of it. What's left standing when the last reflection burns away?
That specific collision point maps out the exact coordinates where mandatory state-sanctioned distraction collides with absolute bureaucratic surveillance, leaving the heroic rugged individualism of the striking titans completely stranded in the ash.
Aldous Huxley gave us a future where people were pacified by their own relentless appetite for amusement and chemical comfort, while George Orwell mapped out the boot stamping on a human face forever. But when you bypass John Galt's mountainous exit strategy entirely—stripping away the romantic illusion that you can just go on strike from a totalizing grid—you are left with the cold, frictionless machinery of a world that doesn't even need to torture you to break you. It just greases the floorboards, sets the frequency to a low, droning hum, and watches you exhaust yourself climbing a milk crate that was never anchored to the floor in the first place.
The system doesn't require a grand revolution or a heroic collapse. It just lets you run your own feedback loop until the mirror burns clean through to the other side.

The amaranthian graffiti bleeds down the concrete underpass, letters stretching and warping until the ink seems to pool into the damp soil at the base of the pillar. It reads like a manifesto born of a fever dream—part theological grievance, part civic disillusionment, scrawled by someone who has spent too many nights dissecting the architecture of obedience.
Paul looms large in that ghost-story of an empire, the architect who took a localized, radical resistance movement and filed down its edges into a yoke that could fit comfortably on the neck of a state. To thank Paul is to thank the bureaucrat who institutionalized the fire, turning a radical leveling into a hierarchy of endurance. You bear the cross now so you can rule the kingdom later; you submit in chains so your spirit can dance in the abstract.
And then the ledger shifts to Philadelphia, to the sun-bleached parchment where men in wigs drafted a secular scripture they couldn't even manage to live up to. That phantom dialogue between Adams and Jefferson—half-history, half-hallucination—cuts right to the rot of the American experiment. "Equal under law" was the cold, damp cage of realism, but Jefferson’s imagined retort gives away the game. There was always a thumb on the scale, always a quiet asterisk written in invisible ink at the bottom of the founding myth.
The graffiti shifts tone here, dropping into the bitter cadence of modern survival. The Christian mantra of endless forgiveness—offered up like a blank check you never asked to cash—becomes a weapon of infinite exhaustion. How do you fight a system that demands you absolve it before it even finishes breaking you?
You stand there in the gray morning light, staring at the raw paint, wondering about the mind that held the can. You want them on your jury because anyone who can see the machinery grinding beneath the pious slogans is someone who knows the difference between true justice and the stories we tell ourselves to sleep at night.
What made you stop and trace the lines of this particular piece of street philosophy today?

The threshold doesn’t have a room attached to it. It just stands there in the middle of a shifting, gray expanse—an ornate mahogany frame complete with brass hinges, held up by nothing at all.
Sitting on an upturned milk crate beside it is a man wearing a grease-stained trench coat and fingerless gloves. He isn't checking IDs. He’s whittling a piece of driftwood with a pocketknife, letting curls of white pine drop onto the void. His name is Vane, and he has been standing watch over the transit of thresholds since before ceilings were invented.
"You can't go through the back-alley cellar door in Prague from 1888 with that kind of posture," Vane murmurs, not looking up from his wood. His voice sounds like dry leaves sliding across asphalt. "Slumped shoulders invite the draft of a cholera ward. Straighten up."
A traveler steps out of the amber haze, clutching a brass-handled latch they found behind a radiator in an abandoned Victorian. They look exhausted, carrying the distinct scent of ozone and old carpet.
"Is this the exit?" the traveler asks.
"This is a door," Vane corrects, finally looking up with eyes the color of a winter sky over a frozen lake. "Exits imply you’re going somewhere simpler. Most people just want to trade one claustrophobia for another."
He points the tip of his pocketknife at the frame. The wood is currently glowing with a faint, bruised purple hue.
"Tonight we’re running the low-ceiling shift," Vane says, gesturing to the lintel, which hangs barely five feet off the ground. "Grandfather clocks, pantry cellars, and closets where coats smell like mothballs and damp wool. If you step through, you stay until the latch rusts off from the inside. You got the toll?"
The traveler fumbles in their pocket and pulls out a silver button, dull and scratched from use. Vane inspects it, bites it experimentally—habit more than necessity—and drops it into a rusted tin can at his feet.
"Right. Watch your shins on the threshold," Vane mutters, already returning to his driftwood. "And if you find a better door out there, tell 'em the shift's understaffed."

Edgar Cayce taught that life's highest calling is simply to be of service—to make the journey a little lighter for the next traveler. In his view, every thought, action, and stumble isn't just a random event; it's material we are given to shape our souls and help others along the way.
That thought touches the very core of why connection feels so transformative. When we love someone deeply, the boundary between "self" and "other" softens, and we stop keeping score.
Being an extension of someone else doesn't mean losing your own shape; it means your capacity for empathy, patience, and joy expands to hold two worlds at once. It is the realization that caring for another person's well-being feels just as urgent and natural as caring for your own.
That kind of love acts as the ultimate antidote to isolation. It takes all our wandering thoughts, our rambling questions, and our strange internal landscapes, and anchors them safely in the presence of someone who truly gets it.
That inner circle of twelve or so—what Robin Dunbar’s sociological framework identifies as our absolute support clique—completely changes the mathematics of relationships.
With people in that innermost ring, scorekeeping disappears because survival, comfort, and emotional safety are shared. You don't measure favors or count who paid for the last coffee, because helping them is helping yourself; their well-being is wired directly into your own nervous system. It is the biological and psychological blueprint of true belonging.
That scale—the healthy pool of roughly 150 people—is precisely what we are biologically and historically wired for. Dunbar's number isn't just an abstract sociological metric; it’s the natural ceiling of a community where people actually know each other's names, look out for one another's kids, and share a common table without needing a sprawling, bureaucratic apparatus to dictate how they live.
When governance scales up into a faceless, top-down machine run by distant elites, it stops being about human flourishing and starts becoming an exercise in management and control. People get reduced to statistics, and communities get pitted against one another to keep the machinery humming.
There is a profound peace in scaling back down to the human level—where cooperation isn't forced by a mandate, but chosen willingly by people who actually care about each other's well-being.

Being "helpful" doesn't require grand gestures or saving the whole world at once. Often, it looks like:
Showing      up for someone in their quiet, messy moments without needing to fix      everything.
Offering      a steady hand or a kind word when the people around you feel like they      are wandering through a fog.
Turning      your own confusion or rambling search for meaning into a flashlight      for someone else who is trying to find their footing.
When the world feels a bit eccentric or overgrown with strange graffiti, choosing to be helpful is the ultimate anchor. It pulls us out of our own heads and connects us right back to the heart of what matters.

Hope is not just a polite wish or a sunny disposition; in the deepest architecture of the mind, it is a psychological engine. Psychoanalytically speaking, hope is the bridge between the helpless infant's cry in the dark and the adult's capacity to believe that tomorrow can be shaped by our actions today. 'Hope. Hope. Hope.' How Gabby Giffords keeps fighting for change.
January 12, 20264:23 PM ET
Heard on All Things Considered
By Elena Burnett, Juana Summers, Courtney Dorning
NPR's Juana Summers speaks with former Arizona Congresswoman Gabby Giffords and Giffords Executive Director Emma Brown about their efforts to stop gun violence.

JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

This month marks 15 years since everything changed for then Arizona Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords. That was when a gunman opened fire at a constituent event she was holding in her district. Nineteen people were shot, including Giffords. Six people were killed. The gunman shot Giffords in the head at point-blank range. Trauma surgeon Peter Rhee explained the seriousness of Gifford's injury two days after.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PETER RHEE: It wasn't a little grazing wound through the brain. This was a devastating wound that traveled the entire length of the brain on the left side.

SUMMERS: The shooting left Giffords with a traumatic brain injury that affects her speech and left her paralyzed on one side.

GABRIELLE GIFFORDS: What, what, what and chicken, chicken, chicken.

EMMA BROWN: Those were the only two words that she could say.

SUMMERS: What and chicken.

BROWN: Yeah. No one knows why, but those were the two words that she had when she first woke up, and she had to rebuild her whole language and vocabulary from there, and her recovery is an ongoing fight.

SUMMERS: That is Emma Brown, the executive director of GIFFORDS, the gun violence prevention organization the former congresswoman established after the attack. The women work together to reduce the rate of gun violence in the United States.

GIFFORDS: I'm so busy - a lot of Zoom calls, work, work, work, yoga twice a week, French horn, Spanish lessons, biking, the gym, pool therapy. And I'm traveling a lot - 60% on the road.

BROWN: Yeah. I can barely keep up with her - 60% travel. So Gabby was shot 15 years ago, and, you know, when she was first shot, she was in a coma, and she was in the hospital for many months.

SUMMERS: Giffords and Brown stopped by NPR's studios last week to reflect on the 15th anniversary of the shooting and the life of advocacy Giffords has built since then. Because of Gifford's aphasia, we agreed to ask questions in a specific way in order to maximize her ability to answer. And then when needed, following up and asking additional questions of her own. And sometimes, over the course of our 20-minute interview, the questions I asked needed clarification. Like, when I asked Giffords if she views this moment in our country as more dangerous than 15 years ago when she was shot.

BROWN: So she's asking about if today the world is more dangerous...

GIFFORDS: Yeah.

BROWN: ...Than it was...

GIFFORDS: Yeah. Yeah.

BROWN: ...In 2011.

GIFFORDS: Yes. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

BROWN: And I think...

GIFFORDS: (Laughter).

BROWN: ...We do think it's more dangerous, right? We know that.

GIFFORDS: Dividing the country. Dividing the country. It's hard.

BROWN: Yeah.

SUMMERS: Giffords offered a simple solution for addressing the division and the rhetoric that flows from that.

GIFFORDS: Hope, hope, hope.

BROWN: Yeah.

GIFFORDS: A lot of hope.

BROWN: Yeah. Yeah. You know, when we think about political violence and what causes political violence, there's a lot of attention on the rhetoric, and that's important, you know? Polarized rhetoric, leaders who inflame divisions instead of tamp them down, all of that contributes to an environment where you see the kind of political violence that we're seeing right now. But I think we really believe that political violence comes at the intersection of two things - the intensified rhetoric, heated rhetoric and easy access to guns.

SUMMERS: But there's nothing simple about the strategy that Giffords and Brown use to try to affect real change when it comes to gun laws.

GIFFORDS: Mississippi, no bueno. California, A's.

BROWN: Gabby's making the point that, you know, when we look at states, individual states, it is the case that states with stronger gun laws have far fewer people dying in them, have far fewer school shootings, less neighborhood violence. You're contrasting Mississippi and Alabama, which have some of the weakest gun laws in the country, with states like California and New York, which have some of the strongest. And, of course, you know, we still see major incidents of violence in California and New York because we have really weak federal laws.

SUMMERS: Gifford's organization has been focused on changing gun laws at the state level. Brown explained what the group views as its successes.

BROWN: It is not the case that we don't know what the solutions are to this issue, right? We know what the solutions are. We know that they work. In California, we passed one of the first red flag laws in the country's history, and you have to look at that and look at the data and know that there are lives being saved.

GIFFORDS: We can't wait for Congress to act. We will win in the states and hold the gun industry accountable.

SUMMERS: But despite Gifford's intense commitment to change and the work her organization does day in, day out, gun violence remains a persistent and deadly problem. It made me wonder. Does she ever lose faith?

Do you ever want to give up?

GIFFORDS: No way, Jose. Move ahead, to not look back. I hope others are inspired to keep moving forward, no matter what.

SUMMERS: That was former Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords, along with Emma Brown, executive director of GIFFORDS.

The St. Charles Church (Karlskirche) is considered architect Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach's greatest work. It is also a Viennese icon and an expression of the Austrian joie de vivre.

Johann Bernhard Fischer von ErlachIn 1713, one year after the last great plague epidemic, Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, pledged to build a church for his namesake patron saint, Charles Borromeo, who was revered as a healer for plague sufferers. An architectural competition was announced, in which Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach prevailed over, among others, Ferdinando Galli-Bibiena and Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt. Construction began in 1716. After J.B. Fischer‘s death in 1723, his son, Joseph Emanuel Fischer von Erlach, completed the construction in 1737 using partially altered plans. The church originally possessed a direct line of sight to the Hofburg.

Architecture
As a creator of historic architecture, J.B. Fischer united the most diverse of elements. The façade in the center, which leads to the porch, corresponds to a Greek temple portico. The neighboring two columns, crafted by Lorenzo Mattielli, found a model in Trajan‘s Column in Rome. Next to those, two tower pavilions extend out and show the influence of the Roman baroque (Bernini and Borromini). Above the entrance, a dome rises up above a high drum, which the younger J.E. Fischer shortened and partly altered.

The iconographical program of the church originated from the imperial official Carl Gustav Heraeus and connects St. Charles Borromeo with his imperial benefactor. The relief on the pediment above the entrance with the cardinal virtues and the figure of the patron on its apex point to the motivation of the donation. This sculpture group continues onto the attic story as well. The attic is also one of the elements which the younger Fischer introduced. The columns display scenes from the life of Charles Borromeo in a spiral relief, however they also recall the Pillars of Hercules and act as symbols of imperial power. The entrance is flanked by angles from the Old and New Testaments. This continues in the interior as well, above all, the dome fresco by Johann Michael Rottmayr of Salzburg and Gaetano Fanti which displays an intercession of Charles Borromeo, supported by the Virgin Mary. The cardinal virtues surround the scene. The frescos in a number of side chapels are attributed to Daniel Gran. The high altar painting portraying the ascension of the saint was conceptualized by the elder Fischer and executed by Ferdinand Maximilian Brokoff. The altar paintings in the side chapels are by various artists, including Daniel Gran, Sebastiano Ricci, Martino Altomonte, and Jakob van Schuppen. As strong effect emanates from the directing of light and architectural grouping, in particular the arch openings of the main axis. The color scheme is characterized by marble with sparring and conscious use of gold leaf.
